stories.title: How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
stories.summary: ShipStation Global's engineering team built Deckhand, an AI IT help desk agent for Slack on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It answers routine IT questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and files Jira tickets. In its first three months it resolved 97.5% of channel queries with a 96% positive feedback rating.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: This post is co-written with Kenneth Salmon, Edward Boswell, Jack Armstrong, Robert Banh, and Nick Ciubotariu from ShipStation Global. Answering the same IT questions and clearing routine tickets drains time that IT teams could spend elsewhere. To reclaim it, the ShipStation Global Engineering team built Deckhand , an AI-powered IT help desk agent for Slack, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . ShipStation Global is the leading intelligent shipping and logistics platform for small and mid-sized shippers, and it operates on a simple belief: the more efficient its teams are, the better it delivers for customers. Deckhand puts that belief to work. It answers routine IT and company questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and creates and updates Jira Service Management tickets. In this post, we discuss how ShipStation architected Deckhand, which resulted in resolving 97.5 percent of incoming channel queries while earning a 96 percent positive feedback rating by employees (Figure 1). Figure 1: 3-month channel coverage and positive feedback The problem Deckhand solves is the one every IT team will recognize: the same questions are routinely asked, error messages are posted after business hours, and information needs to be gathered from different teams. At ShipStation Global, those conversations lived in a busy help desk Slack channel, where employees asked, and IT answered, one thread at a time. The answers usually already existed in a Confluence how-to article, on a company intranet page, or in a thread from eight months earlier. Finding them was the hard part. The channel data made the scale concrete. In the 12 months before launch: “We created Deckhand because getting help should be as simple as asking a question in Slack, not deciphering a ticket form or sending an email into the void. We believe that tickets are an indication of operational friction not productivity. Deckhand resolves common questions on the spot and, when it can’t, converts the conversation into a fully contextualized ticket with one click, improving the employee experience and freeing our team from endlessly repeating the phrase: ‘Please file a ticket.’” — Chris Collins, Senior Director IT at ShipStation Global Deckhand works in Slack like any teammate—joining channels, reading the conversation, and drawing context from Slack profiles to answer IT questions in place. We run it on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, hosts the agent in isolated sessions, so we run no servers or containers. The solution has four main components, shown in Figure 2: Figure 2: Architecture diagram showing Slack events entering the Slack service and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, with separate paths to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, AgentCore Gateway-backed Lambda tools, Jira Service Management, and DynamoDB feedback. When an employee posts in a channel where Deckhand is a member, the Slack service assembles the full thread history and user context. It then invokes the agent through the AgentCore runtime API. The agent searches the knowledge base and calls tools as needed. When it finds an answer, it returns a final response (Figure 3). When it doesn’t, it asks a clarifying question or offers to create a ticket (Figure 4). Figure 3: Deckhand responds with self-service steps Figure 4: Deckhand offers to create a ticket This section walks through how Deckhand is implemented, from prerequisites to a working deployment. To implement this pattern, you need the following: The agent is intentionally lightweight. Using the open source Strands Agents SDK , an agent consists of a model, a set of tools, and a system prompt. The SDK manages the reasoning loop, allowing the model to select tools, process results, and iterate until it produces an answer. Deckhand’s agent service is implemented in a few lines of Python. The model ID is set through an environment variable, which allows switching models without modifying application code. Tools are integrated with the agent in two ways. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases retrieval is a native Strands tool that supports knowledge base search with a single import. Other functions, including classification, ticket management, user resolution, and image analysis, are handled by a Lambda function registered on AgentCore Gateway. The Gateway exposes these as MCP tools, and the Lambda routes each invocation by tool name. This separation allows tool logic to be updated independently, and the agent can access new tools from the Gateway without requiring a rebuild. AgentCore runtime hosts the agent as a container, avoiding the need for server or session management. The Slack service calls the agent synchronously for each message, providing the thread transcript and user context, and posts the final response. Since context, including the employee’s profile, is included with every request, the agent can complete ticket details automatically. Deckhand answers from a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with core S3-backed data sources: Each document includes metadata such as title, source URL, content type, and event dates. This allows the agent to filter content, for example, when users ask about upcoming events or weekly lunch menus in the Austin office. The most valuable data source is the archive of resolved support threads. Before Deckhand existed, Slack was where problems got solved: years of employees describing issues and IT walking them through fixes. That history is an organic knowledge base, validated by the best possible reviewer: the person whose problem got fixed. It’s also noisy: a raw export mixes banter, automated alerts, and threads that never actually got resolved. sources.title: How Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI technology
sources.text: Block is using AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak to compress the time to fix vulnerabilities, freeing its security team to focus on strategic work. Hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry Minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch Analyst-hours of investigation completed each quarter At Block, the company behind Square, Cash App, and Afterpay, the security team leverages the OpenAI Defense Factory: where AI handles vulnerability discovery, detection, and response at a scale that no human team could keep up with. With AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak, Block is taking just hours to do work that used to take weeks. Block’s security team has been focused on responsibly adopting AI across workflows, whether that’s code generation or security operations. “What it’s really centered on is having a new teammate that you can scale with,” James Nettesheim, Chief Information Security Officer, says. “It’s not like a more traditional automation where you had to go step by step. You can prompt it with a fairly bespoke, ambiguous problem and work through it together.” Projects like reviewing a software bug or parsing a log would take days or weeks to complete. Now the team can complete those projects in a fraction of the time, with a human still validating every result. For example, for detection tuning, every investigation stores its raw query evidence, so the team can now replay a proposed detection change against seven months of production telemetry in under an hour. That work used to mean requerying hundreds of old cases by hand, and often it rarely happened in practice since it was so time-consuming. The team has also gotten more particular about which model they’re using for which job. “We used to use the latest model, but you don’t need to do that anymore,” he says. “It’s been a learning experience to choose different models for different tasks.” Block’s security harness is built on top of Daybreak to help route tasks to the right model, and it includes hooks for humans to take over tasks or for agents to verify each other’s work. The team continually evaluates these systems against internal benchmarks and real-world performance, adjusting its approach when needed, including routing work to human review when that is the responsible path. The automated triage system has resulted in faster work (and more of it) getting done. Block’s security team has seen a 50% boost to triage throughput, a 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations, and an entirely new autonomous hunting capability. Nettesheim says, “This performs ~1,100 analyst-hours of investigation per quarter, because every alert now gets a full, deep investigation across all elements the alert involves. Our system works every alert like it’s the only alert we’ve got that day.” Traditional scanning tools flag a single vulnerability in isolation, but Block’s security team can go much further with Daybreak. The model helps hypothesize about attack patterns and chain together a series of attacks into a full end-to-end compromise path, surfacing vulnerabilities that might have existed for years. In one case, an alert on a single laptop looked like a minor policy issue on its own. But during peer review, the model followed an indicator that appeared only incidentally in the evidence, joined it against Block’s identity logs, and surfaced a much larger set of issues. “One routine endpoint alert became a campaign takedown. No single tool makes that join. The signal only exists across two products’ logs,” James says. Another example when Daybreak helped was during a recent red team exercise. The model was given a few hints about an internal system, and it chained together a full attack path—SQL injection, privilege escalation, a foothold, credential enumeration, and a pivot to other systems—in about two hours. This would typically take a human red teamer several days. In recent red team exercises, the time from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch was 18 minutes. Finding the vulnerabilities is only as good as the ability to fix them. Nettesheim walks through the process his team uses on every finding: locate where the issue lives in the code and identify who owns it, then move to remediation. “You propose a patch, you confirm exploitability, and then you verify that you have fixed it, with a human in the loop guiding it and deploying the code changes.” While agents are technically capable, they don’t carry an organization’s context or the reasoning behind previous decisions. A human provides that context and strategy, and that’s where his team comes in to provide a human layer of review. As AI’s judgment is proven out in practice, Nettesheim says, “we’ll slowly ladder up the risk level to use it for more sensitive systems.” Less than one hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry. 18 minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch in recent red team exercises. Roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter of false-positive triage handed back. Approximately 1,100 analyst-hours of investigation completed per quarter. 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations. Detection and response work alone has handed back roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter that used to go toward triaging false positives. With that time back, the team now spends more time on deeper investigations and building more automation responsibly. As the pace of attack increases and AI models keep advancing, Nettesheim sees an opportunity to reduce the number of vulnerabilities introduced in the first place. sources.title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
sources.text: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline: When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement. That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time. Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate. Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to. Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows. For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first. Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet. Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. stories.title: Higgsfield takes AI video from 1 minute to over 10
stories.summary: Higgsfield brings creators longer videos with GPT-6 Astra, precise visuals with GPT-Image-2.5, and a path to voice filmmaking with GPT-Live.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: Higgsfield takes AI video from 1 minute to over 10
sources.text: Higgsfield brings creators longer videos with GPT‑6 Astra, precise visuals with GPT‑Image‑2.5, and a path to voice filmmaking with GPT‑Live. Higgsfield AI ⁠ (opens in a new window) is on a mission to make professional video and image creation accessible to anyone with an idea. Before GPT‑6 Astra, those videos topped out at around one minute. Now, says CEO and co-founder Alex Mashrabov, users can create videos over 10 minutes long. Longer videos are just one way Higgsfield AI helps smaller creative teams take on more ambitious work. According to Alex, with models like GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, it’s now possible for a single creator to execute high-end fashion campaigns from start to finish. Higgsfield AI’s creative agents take on repetitive production tasks, such as creating multiple variations of a shot. With GPT‑6 Astra, those agents can also call external tools to handle complex, manual work in 3D modeling. Alex says that capability helps address one of creative AI’s hardest problems: maintaining consistency across longer videos. The evidence can be seen on Higgsfield AI’s own YouTube channel, which Alex says has almost half a million subscribers. The channel teaches creatives how to use AI models and workflows. It used to require considerable manual effort for Higgsfield AI to produce that content. But with GPT‑6 Astra, the team has built a workflow that uses AI to generate instructional videos over 10 minutes long. Being able to create longer instructional videos also matters to Alex personally. He supports rural schools in Kazakhstan and describes an early effort using GPT‑6 Astra’s visual understanding to identify topics students may be struggling with and create videos tailored to what they need to learn. For small businesses creating promotional content, having readable text and precise infographics can be just as important as the image itself. GPT‑Image‑2.5 makes that kind of content possible for businesses without large production budgets, Alex says. “GPT‑Image‑2.5 is state of the art and the first model of its kind that can reliably render the text and infographics on top of the imagery,” he says. Higgsfield AI builds its product through close collaboration between around 200 creatives and 100 engineers. Codex gives the creative team “the power of a really strong software engineer,” shares Alex. Creatives use Codex to turn their ideas into software prototypes. Previously, bringing those prototypes into production required heavy involvement from front-end and back-end engineers. Now, Alex says GPT‑6 Astra reduces the work needed to bring those ideas into the product. With less friction between prototyping and production, Alex says Higgsfield AI can develop and ship better products faster. Next, Higgsfield AI wants creators to be able to describe an idea and see it take shape as they talk. Alex calls that vision “voice to movie,” with AI understanding a creator’s spoken intention and rendering their vision in real time. He sees OpenAI’s advances in planning, tool calling, image generation, and voice bringing that experience closer. He describes its voice model as “best in class for voice understanding and just for regular communication.” For Higgsfield AI, the ambition is to make creating a film feel more like describing an idea, with AI handling more of the work in between.

stories.title: Leading Tech Companies Join Global Law Enforcement in Major Crackdown on West African Scam Networks
stories.summary: Meta and 14 other tech companies joined law enforcement from ten countries to disrupt scam networks operating in West Africa in the largest operation of its kind to date. The post Leading Tech Companies Join Global Law Enforcement in Major Crackdown on West African Scam Networks appeared first on Meta Newsroom .

sources.name: Meta Newsroom
sources.title: Leading Tech Companies Join Global Law Enforcement in Major Crackdown on West African Scam Networks
sources.text: Today, Meta, Coinbase, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, Starlink, Adobe, and other leading tech companies announced the results of a major joint operation with law enforcement to disrupt criminal scam networks based in West African nations, including Nigeria and Ghana. Hosted by the National Crime Agency (NCA) in London in partnership with the US Department of Justice, the FBI, and several US federal agencies, the operation marked the latest and largest instance of tech companies coming together with law enforcement around the world to share information, take down sophisticated criminals, and help protect people from online scams. This is the first joint disruption to broadly target criminal scam networks in the West Africa region. Scam centers based in Nigeria, Ghana, and other nations in the region are generally more decentralized and less industrial than those in southeast Asia. Criminals are continually seeking new havens where they believe they can operate with impunity, and it’s essential that law enforcement, industry, and government work together to disrupt these criminals wherever they may try to organize and operate. Beginning Tuesday, October 6, the NCA — in coordination with the FBI, the US Department of Justice, Homeland Security Investigations and other US agencies — convened Meta and other leading tech companies at NCA headquarters in London along with Ghanaian law enforcement, Nigerian law enforcement, and other law enforcement partners from Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and India. The disruption kicked off with remarks from law enforcement leaders that included a call to action from Jeanine Pirro, US Attorney for the District of Columbia and leader of the US Department of Justice Scam Center Strike Force. Other participating US agencies included the US Secret Service, US Department of Treasury, and the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF). Over the following days, teams shared actionable intelligence to connect information across platforms, jurisdictions, and financial systems in order to identify and target criminal networks at multiple points along the fraud attack chain. Their activity ranged from scammer recruitment and infrastructure to victim identification and the movement of funds, with a majority targeting the US but also reaching people in the UK and around the world. Disrupting these criminal centers resulted in the rescue of 117 individuals who had been trafficked to work against their will in scam compounds in Ghana. These victims had been forced to work for scam operations by criminal syndicates and were rescued from imprisonment in a residential compound. The victims were malnourished and subjected to both physical and psychological abuses by their captors, who were arrested and are facing prosecution. This operation identified and disrupted a range of fraud types connected to these networks, including: “Scams are a global threat that demand a global response. Last week, working with the UK National Crime Agency, the FBI, DOJ, and the Homeland Security Task Force, we took the fight to scam centers across West Africa. As part of the disruption, we removed more than 3.7 million accounts, Pages and Groups targeting people in the US, UK, and beyond, and shared leads on over 30 suspected scam centers resulting in dozens of arrests, the rescue of trafficking victims, and cryptocurrency seizures. This operation shows what partnership makes possible, and we’ll keep working with law enforcement and industry to pursue scammers wherever they operate.” — Chris Sonderby, VP and Deputy General Counsel, Meta “Fraud is a global problem and it takes partnership working across international boundaries to tackle it. Hosting such a rich and dedicated team of law enforcement and technology companies at NCA’s headquarters enabled us to utilize the power of partnerships and strike back at a significant set of criminals who inflict misery on thousands of victims of fraud. Fraudsters can operate from anywhere and will target victims both domestically and globally. The NCA will continue to work with international and private sector partners to tackle fraudsters working upstream, overseas, and online. Collaborating in this way sends a clear signal to criminals that the combined capabilities of law enforcement and industry means that we will relentlessly pursue them and the infrastructure they rely on no matter where they operate.” — Nick Sharp, Deputy Director of Fraud at the National Crime Agency “Thanks to brilliant partnership with the Department of Justice and the private sector, across multiple African countries, we arrested dozens of criminal actors, seized hundreds of devices, identified at least $11 million in potentially freezable funds, and truly saved lives. This is what happens when law enforcement executes with precision across the interagency. We are demolishing Scam Centers across the globe and crushing a criminal industry preying on American citizens.” “Transnational fraud demands a transnational response. I have partnered with the NCA and the Crown Prosecutor for England and Wales to push forward cases on both sides of the Atlantic; criminals are not hindered by borders and neither are we. We will deploy our team wherever in the world transnational criminals target innocent victims.” — Jeanine Ferris Pirro, US Attorney for the District of Columbia, Founder of the Scam Center Strike Force “Criminal gangs operating overseas are behind most of the scams targeting the British public. That is why these multi-agency operations are critical, and my thanks go to all the officers involved in intercepting and arresting these scammers. Our new Online Crime Centre will build on this work to dismantle criminal networks and bring offenders to justice, wherever in the world they might be.” “Fraud networks now run at industrial scale, using AI to target victims and move proceeds across chains faster than any manual process can follow. stories.summary: Announcing the Official Selection for the Edits Film Festival happening in Mumbai this week. The post Announcing the Official Selection for the Edits Film Festival appeared first on Meta Newsroom .

sources.name: Meta Newsroom
sources.title: Announcing the Official Selection for the Edits Film Festival
sources.text: Today we’re announcing the Official Selection for the Edits Film Festival , happening in Mumbai this week. The festival was announced in August to recognize creative talent across India — especially those who use editing as their superpower to make their content stand out. From August 25 to October 8, we invited you to create something meaningful from your camera roll. It could be entertaining, informative, or strike an emotional chord in any other way. The festival drew over 200 entries from across India. Some focused on genres like humor, some on formats like vlogs and GRWM, and some were deep works of fiction. The films selected weren’t just great stories – they also showed what the Edits app can do. The selection was made by a diverse group of people at Meta, along with the teams at Yuvaa, with whom the festival was co-curated. Here are the 12 Official Selections in no particular order: The top three submissions will be chosen by a talented panel of judges — Ahsaas Channa, Dolly Singh, Nikhil Taneja and Rajeev Masand. Follow all the updates with #EditsFilmFestival .

sources.name: Meta Newsroom
sources.title: Farah Khan at Edits Film Festival: “Content breakthroughs come from spontaneity, relatability and realness”
sources.text: Today the curtains came down on the Edits Film Festival in Mumbai, in the presence of filmmaker Farah Khan, festival judges Ahsaas Channa, Dolly Singh, Nikhil Taneja and Rajeev Masand and over 100 content creators in the audience. The festival awarded its winners – Ishank Gupta ( @filmmaker.ishank ), Sanya Rohillaa ( @bunniestbunnytoeverbunnny ) and Ahsan Vazir ( @ahsan_vazir__ ) for their great storytelling and use of Edits for editing their content. Submissions for the Edits Film Festival commenced in August, where in a duration of 45 days, you were encouraged to submit a piece of content made from unpolished videos in your camera roll, and edited using Edits, Instagram’s video editing app. While the Official Selection played at the festival demonstrated this, the top three in particular, selected by the jury, displayed a rare sense of adventure, restraint and skill. The top three submissions, by Ishank Gupta ( @filmmaker.ishank ), Sanya Rohillaa ( @bunniestbunnytoeverbunnny ) and Ahsan Vazir ( @ahsan_vazir__ ), stood out for diverse storytelling, and use of Edits features in them. The winners were selected by Ahsaas Channa, Dolly Singh, Nikhil Taneja and Rajeev Masand. “Enabling creators with the right tools, platforms and opportunities is central to what we do. The festival opened up new creative possibilities, encouraging creators to experiment with features they hadn’t used before and tell stories in fresh ways. We’re thankful to our jury members and to Farah Khan for the invaluable perspective she shared on her storytelling journey.” – Ankit Rihal, Head of Global Partnerships, Meta, India Film maker Farah Khan was the special guest at the event, who spoke about her approach to content creation and film making, which is a rare combination of someone who’s made feature films for theatres, as well as online content for Reels. “People assume there’s a big plan behind it, but I don’t overthink what I post. Gen Z has inspired me — they’re so nonchalant about it, no second-guessing. Be it a clip from my show, a random chat or a bit of mischief on the spot, everything is spontaneous for me. I think relatability and realness, with a bit of humor, are what audiences actually respond to on Instagram.” – Farah Khan Follow @metaindia and #EditsFilmFestival for seeing more updates from the event.

stories.title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI
stories.summary: AWS engineers share kernel optimizations for fused Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on Amazon SageMaker AI: Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization, Triton backend routing for FP8 quantization, and eliminating Triton JIT recompilation. Together they deliver up to 10% higher throughput and up to 9% faster Time to First Token on H200 GPUs.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI
sources.text: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a sparsely-activated architecture that scales large language model (LLM) capacity while keeping per-token compute low. Because its operations account for a large share of total compute time, inefficiencies there directly raise request latency and cost. Therefore, optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains. Fused MoE is a key optimization technique for the MoE architecture. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. This replaces executing those routing and expert computations as separate, sequential loop operations. While this provides latency advantages, it also brings complexity in kernel implementations and debugging capability. High GPU utilization for this architecture requires hardware-specific optimizations. In this post, we describe the different kernel optimizations we implemented for fused MoE models and show you how you can benefit from this work. We used a representative MoE model as our primary example. To maximize tensor processing throughput, the NVIDIA Hopper architecture relies on the Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction protocol, which executes collectively across a cooperative warpgroup of 128 threads. This operand asymmetry is fundamentally an instruction set architecture (ISA)-level property. In the underlying wgmma.mma_async assembly definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension (M) at a constant scale of 64 to define its parallel thread-mapping topology. The column dimension (N) remains highly variable. Operand A strictly maps across this fixed M dimension (using registers or shared memory), and Operand B maps across the variable N dimension (through a shared memory descriptor). These operand slots are therefore structurally non-interchangeable. Consequently, peak hardware tile utilization is governed by these rigid shape encodings, requiring that the M dimension equals or exceeds 64 to prevent compute execution lanes from sitting idle. This structural preference stems from how Hopper Tensor Cores partition memory blocks. The hardware enforces a fixed minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 (M=64). When a mathematical matrix possesses a large, continuous leading dimension in this primary slot, Hopper’s internal hardware schedulers can cleanly map and distribute data across the physical computing grid. This structural asymmetry becomes a severe performance bottleneck during the decode phase of MoE networks. In a standard MoE layer, the linear algebra governing expert computation is formulated using traditional matrix notation: Where (M) represents the token row count (or batch size), (K) represents the hidden feature dimension, and (N) represents the expansive expert output dimension. During the decode phase, the system processes only one token per user sequence at a time. Consequently, the batch space or token row size is profoundly thin, regularly dropping to a profile where (M < 64), and frequently down to a single row (M = 1). Under this standard structural layout: Matrix (A) transforms into a thin, fragmented horizontal vector (for example, 1 x 4096). Matrix (B) (the core expert weights) remains in a large, dense vertical block (for example, 4096 x 8192). Because the row count (M) is tiny, Matrix (A) is physically incapable of filling the hardware’s fixed (64)-row layout bucket for Operand A. When the WGMMA instruction executes over this layout, it leaves a vast portion of the physical Tensor Core capacity completely starved. The silicon spends clock cycles processing empty spatial slots, leading to poor hardware utilization. In a standard dense LLM layer, weight matrices are static, unified, and perfectly contiguous. In an MoE layer, however, the workload is fractured across a fleet of independent subnetworks (experts). This creates unique memory and layout bottlenecks that make it hypersensitive to the WGMMA constraints of the Hopper GPU. In a standard dense layer, matrix multiplication multiplies a token vector by a single layer weight matrix. The output dimension (N) is the model’s hidden size (for example, 4096). In a Fused MoE kernel, the GPU isn’t only multiplying against one expert. It’s grouping and running math for all active experts simultaneously to avoid launching individual kernels for each expert. For a standard dense layer, N is the hidden size (4,096). For a fused MoE layer, N is the number of experts chosen multiplied by the expert intermediate size. For a model running a topk=8 routine, the effective N dimension inside the fused kernel explodes into tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters. Because the N dimension is so disproportionately large compared to the tiny decode token size (M=1), the layout asymmetry becomes extreme. Transposing the matrices moves this large, combined MoE dimension into the primary slot, unlocking hardware prefetching at a scale that standard dense layers cannot match. To resolve this hardware misalignment without altering the underlying mathematical integrity of the model, we exploit the algebraic property of matrix transposition: By programmatically flipping the matrix multiplication before it reaches the PTX assembly layer, we realigned the software to match the exact topography of the Hopper silicon. This transposition triggers two immediate architectural advantages on the GPU. First, it saturates the physical layout. The expansive expert dimension (N = 8192) is promoted to the first operand position (B T ), and because (N) is large it easily floods the hardware’s mandatory (64)-row threshold. The Tensor Cores then operate at maximum local density with no wasted execution cycles. Second, it activates asynchronous prefetching. Hopper’s dedicated hardware copy engines can prefetch memory addresses asynchronously from shared memory

stories.title: Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock
stories.summary: Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock. In this post, we build a tool-calling agent on Grok 4.7 and evaluate it on three reasoning tasks at four reasoning effort levels, measuring correctness and token cost per completed task. We show how to tune the trade-off per request and monitor it in production.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock
sources.text: SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock, which offers a choice of foundation models (FMs) from multiple providers. According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 is trained to work longer on more difficult tasks and knows when to check its own work. That matters most for agents, which carry a task through many steps and must verify what they find along the way. An agent that works this way has to do more than look things up. It has to form a candidate answer, check it against what it has learned, and refine it until it fits. Grok 4.7 exposes a reasoning effort setting that controls how much deliberation happens before each response, and for agent workloads a practical question is which level to run. In this post, we build a tool-calling agent on Grok 4.7 and evaluate it on three tasks that require search rather than lookup. The tasks are diagnosing a two-service outage from its alerts, scheduling maintenance under interacting constraints, and choosing an optimal set of migrations under a budget. Each task has exactly one correct answer, verified by brute force. We ran all three at every reasoning effort level, six times each, for 72 agent runs. The agent answered 67 of the 72 runs correctly. At xhigh it answered all 18 correctly, and at low it answered 15 of 18 while using about an eighth of the output tokens. That gives a clear trade-off you can tune per request, and we show how to measure it on your own tasks and how to monitor it in production. We report token counts rather than currency throughout. Token prices change, and the counts are what your own costs are derived from, so a measurement expressed in tokens stays valid. According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 uses a larger base model than Grok 4.6 and was trained with a longer reinforcement learning run on a harder mix of tasks. This mix is weighted toward problems that take many hours to complete. SpaceXAI reports that the model is better at verifying its own work and at managing longer context. SpaceXAI’s published benchmark results follow that emphasis. The largest reported gains over Grok 4.6 appear in the categories that measure sustained work rather than single-turn answers. Source: SpaceXAI, Introducing Grok 4.7 ( https://x.ai/news/grok-4-7 ). Scores are as published by SpaceXAI at the time of the model launch. Benchmarks show how a model performs across standard tasks. For your own workload, the useful next step is to measure on tasks shaped like yours, which is what the rest of this post walks through. SpaceXAI lists a 500K token context window for Grok 4.7, with text and image input and text output. On Amazon Bedrock, the model supports configurable reasoning effort, tool calling, and structured output. Grok 4.7 runs on the bedrock-runtime endpoint and is accessed through a cross-Region inference profile. Two profiles are available: Cross-Region inference routes requests across multiple AWS Regions, which gives you higher throughput without managing capacity Region by Region. Requests name one of the inference profiles rather than a bare model ID. The model supports the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. On Converse, reasoning is returned as a reasoningContent block alongside the text block. In inferenceConfig , set maxTokens only, and put model-specific parameters, such as reasoning effort, in additionalModelRequestFields . For the current list of supported Regions, service tiers, and token prices, see the Grok 4.7 model card in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page ( https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/ ). Your AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity needs bedrock:InvokeModel on both the inference profile and your account’s default project: Include both resources in the policy statement. The default project permission is required in addition to the inference profile. For production use, we recommend generating a short-term bearer token from your existing AWS credentials, so authentication stays tied to your IAM identity and no long-lived secret is stored: Reasoning tokens count as output tokens and draw down max_completion_tokens before the answer text is produced, so size the limit to leave room for both. If the limit is reached during reasoning, the response returns without answer text, so check for empty content in agent code and raise the limit if you see it. Our runs used a limit of 32,768 tokens, which left headroom at every effort level. Grok 4.7 supports four effort levels: low , medium , high , and xhigh . Effort levels can change between model versions, so it is worth confirming them against the service rather than hardcoding a list: Many agent evaluations test diligence: read a record, filter it, add it up. Those tasks are worth having, but to see what reasoning effort contributes, a task has to require search: the answer can’t be read off the data, it has to be proposed and then checked. We built a synthetic environment of 20 services, exposed through seven tools, and three tasks on top of it. Every task has exactly one correct answer, and each is built so that a quick heuristic is not enough to find it. Four practices keep a measurement like this trustworthy, and they apply to most agent evaluations. State every rule the grader relies on. If the prompt leaves an edge case open, a reasonable answer can be scored as wrong, and the evaluation ends up measuring the specification rather than the model. The diagnosis prompt, for example, says explicitly that a failed service raises no alert of its own. Prove each task has one answer. Each environment is small enough to enumerate, so we checked every candidate answer before running anything. For the schedule, that is a few lines: Grade a required final line, not the whole response. Each prompt asks the agent to end with a line such as FINAL: auth, checkout . The grader reads only that line, so a response that discusses other candidates while explaining its reasoning is grad

sources.title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
sources.text: AI agents increasingly need to access web resources that are priced per request. For example, premium datasets charge by the query, research APIs meter by the call, and paywalled publishers gate content behind payment. When an AI agent encounters one of these resources, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent has no built-in payment mechanism, no budget attached to the session, and no programmatic way to satisfy the request. The task stalls and requires manual intervention. Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine-to-machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent. Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory , it’s now available on AWS Marketplace . This post covers how Anchor Browser integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments so that AI agents can pay for x402-protected pages and APIs autonomously. The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP-based machine-to-machine payments. A server responds with 402 Payment Required along with the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address that the agent uses to complete the transaction. Anchor Browser is a cloud-based browser automation solution purpose-built for AI agents. Each agent session runs inside a managed browser environment that maintains authentication state, handles navigation, captures network requests, and provides a live view of page interactions. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides capabilities to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments is a fully managed capability within AgentCore that AI agents can use to discover, access, and pay for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously. AgentCore payments manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits at the infrastructure layer, and processes payments through the x402 protocol. It also provides observability into payment attempts, approvals, denials, and settlements through Amazon CloudWatch. When an agent running in Anchor Browser encounters a 402 response, AgentCore payments authorizes and completes the transaction within the configured budget. The workflow continues without interruption. When an autonomous agent encounters an x402-protected resource, the workflow stalls. The agent makes a request, such as fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data enrichment API, and the server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. Without a mechanism to pay, the task that was supposed to run autonomously now requires human intervention. Today, developers must build the entire payment stack. This effort spans four categories of complexity: Without a managed payment service, the agent must internalize the entire payment stack. On every x402-protected call that returns a 402 response, the agent must orchestrate the full payment flow internally, including: Each of these steps requires custom code that developers must build, secure, and maintain. Figure 1 illustrates this architecture. The agent contains eight tightly coupled components (Wallet, Private Keys, Budget Controls, Sign Proof, Attach Header, Retry Logic, Settle Payment, and Logging). The agent connects to an x402 API with a 402 challenge flowing back and a retry flowing forward. The security considerations extend beyond the engineering effort. Uncontrolled spending. Without hard spending limits enforced at the infrastructure level, a bug, retry loop, prompt injection, or inadvertent access can trigger unintended payments. An agent retrying a paid endpoint in a loop continues to authorize payments until manual intervention occurs. Key exposure. When private keys reside inside the agent runtime, they share an execution environment with untrusted web pages, third-party tools, and external dependencies. These vectors might inadvertently disclose the credentials that control real funds. Signing flow exposure. If the signing infrastructure is accessible from the runtime, a threat actor can attempt to access the key or redirect payments to an address under unauthorized control. Effective mitigation requires that the key doesn’t enter the runtime in the first place. Browser-based agents introduce an additional constraint: the payment must occur within the same browser session. Otherwise, session recordings and live view no longer match what actually executed. Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments address this complexity by moving the entire payment stack into managed infrastructure. Unlike a stateless tool call, Anchor Browser provides a real cloud browser with persistent identity, repeatable and deterministic workflows, and the session context needed to log in, navigate, and finish tasks reliably. Authentication, navigation, network requests, recordings, and live view happen inside the same browser session. When a payment is required, the transaction happens within that session. The recording captures the full sequence from request to 402 to payment to content delivery. Anchor agents include a built-in x402 tool that handles paid API calls natively within the browser context. The built-in tool requires no changes to existing Playwright, Puppeteer, or Chrome DevTools Protocol-based workflows. AgentCore payments serves as the payment layer. At the center of the service is the Payment Manager, the top-level resource that coordinates payment operations for the AWS account. Creating a Payment Manager requires specifying an authorizer type and an IAM role. AgentCore then provisions a corresponding workload identity in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. The remaining components connect the Payment Manager to external wallet infrastructure: Anchor Browser sets up wallets through AgentCore payments using a supported wallet provider, without placing wallet secrets or private keys inside the agent runtime. AgentCore payments handles wallet operations through the configured provider. For endpoint discovery, AgentCore provides a curated Coinbase x402 Bazaar MCP s

sources.title: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: A financial services team spends significant time each week manually creating client PowerPoint presentations from quarterly reports, compliance documents, and market analyses. Each presentation requires reading hundreds of pages, extracting key data points, structuring slides, and generating supporting visuals. This post walks you through building an AI agent system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this workflow, completing in under 90 seconds in our internal testing. This approach reduces presentation creation time while grounding content in source documents. The solution deploys a supervisor agent on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using the Strands Agents framework to orchestrate document generation and summarization tools. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (available on Amazon Bedrock) handles content creation, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 powers vector search, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available on Amazon Bedrock) generates slide images. This post includes a public repository with the code assets. The solution deploys a single supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that selects between document generation and summarization tools based on user requests. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector storage and semantic search across multimodal content. The solution includes a REST API built with .NET 8 minimal APIs, so you can integrate with existing enterprise applications through standard HTTP calls. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute, including containerized functions for PowerPoint generation. The solution secures the implementation with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) isolation, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) least-privilege access control. This section covers AgentCore runtime, RAG, and content safety guardrails as they apply to this solution. A single AI agent generating documents from large knowledge bases must retrieve content, structure outlines, generate text, create images, and assemble files. Rather than implementing these competing responsibilities in a monolithic function, the solution uses a tool-based architecture where a supervisor agent routes requests to specialized tools. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent code runs in an isolated container with session management, built-in identity, and observability. The solution uses the Strands Agents framework (an open source SDK for building AI agents) to implement the supervisor logic. The agent determines whether a request requires document generation, content summarization, or both, then invokes the appropriate tool. You can add new capabilities by defining new tools in the agent code without modifying existing ones. RAG addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems: delivering accurate, up-to-date information grounded in enterprise data rather than relying solely on the model’s training data. The implementation uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , which combine vector search with large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant context before generating responses. This approach is designed to help reduce hallucinated content by grounding generated documents in source information from the enterprise knowledge base. Note: The Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection data plane must remain publicly accessible because Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases accesses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless from AWS-managed infrastructure, not through customer VPC endpoints. IAM data access policies protect the collection, and VPC-only access restricts the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless dashboard. Enterprise AI applications require content moderation to meet organizational standards and compliance requirements. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers built-in content filtering and safety mechanisms integrated throughout the document generation pipeline. The implementation creates custom guardrails through AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) , configured with specific policies tailored to enterprise document creation. The agent applies guardrails at the model invocation level, providing consistent content safety without requiring manual configuration for each deployment. The following diagram illustrates the agent-based document generation system. Figure 1: Architecture of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore RAG presentation generation system The data flow begins with user requests arriving through Amazon API Gateway , which routes them to a .NET-based Chat API running on AWS Lambda . The API maintains conversation state in Amazon DynamoDB . It then invokes the supervisor agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. The supervisor agent analyzes the request and selects the appropriate tool. For document generation, it invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda (a containerized Python function). For summarization, the supervisor invokes the Summary Generator Lambda, which queries the knowledge base through the retrieve_and_generate API. The system processes, chunks, and embeds documents stored in Amazon S3 using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless indexes the embeddings for fast semantic search. When tools query the knowledge base, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless retrieves relevant chunks, which are then supplied as context to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (on Amazon Bedrock) for generating grounded responses. The system stores generated documents in Amazon S3 and returns presigned URLs for secure download. sources.title: Building trust in AI agents: A production-ready evaluation framework with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: Every organization racing to deploy AI agents faces the same reckoning: an agent that demos beautifully can quietly degrade in production, and by the time a human notices, the trust is already broken. Where traditional software fails loudly, agents fail softly. They return an answer that looks confident, reads fluently, and is wrong. When that answer drives a real business decision, the cost is not a broken feature. It’s a broken relationship with the user. That’s the quality problem at its core. The challenge is therefore not building agents that work once, but proving they keep working, at scale, across every sub-agent, every workflow, and every release. The teams that win the agent era will be the ones who treat quality not as a final QA step but as the operating system of the agent itself: continuously measured, automatically defended, and improved with every interaction. In this post, we show how we built a continuous quality loop for production-ready agentic solutions at scale using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and other AWS services for internal use, so sellers and sales leaders can ask business questions in plain English from Amazon Quick. Behind that single experience, several specialized sub-agents work together: the Performance Insights Agent for territory-scoped revenue and performance, the Customer Insights Agent for customer intelligence, the Data Insights Agent for text-to-SQL over foundational datasets, and direct dashboard access. Answers are scoped to each user’s territory and role-level security. Field teams use these answers to assist in planning account strategy, prepare for customer meetings, so the numbers must be right. The most damaging failure is not a crash. It’s a fluent, confident answer that is quietly wrong. Before launch, when we evaluated the Customer Insights Agent, we found exactly that: Through the different runs, monitoring stayed green. It told us the system had responded, not whether the answer was right. Had these errors shipped uncaught, the field would have paid for them. A seller who repeats an inflated figure can lose credibility with the customer. This is exactly why we caught it before launch. The risk doesn’t end at launch: it grows with every new agent and every change to data, prompts, code, or models. It also grows without any release, because upstream pipelines refresh the data every week. Coordinated releases introduce a related risk: when a data change, a tool change, and a paired prompt update are meant to ship together but land apart, the system runs mismatched until all changes catch up. In one pre-production test, that mismatch window by itself dropped the pass rate from 78 percent to 38 percent. To catch failures like these, before every release and continuously in production, we need a framework that can show whether answers are grounded and correct, and trace each failure back to its root cause in the data, the prompt, or the agent’s code. At AWS, the Sales, Marketing, and Global Services (SMGS) Operations team developed a production multi-agent system serving AWS Field Sales worldwide. It serves two distinct audiences. For field sales teams, it replaces hours of manual data analysis with on-demand, conversational intelligence, helping sellers understand the health of their business, surface risks and opportunities, and take action faster. For leadership, it powers business management cadences including Weekly Business Reviews (WBRs), surfacing the signals that matter across the portfolio without requiring manual report preparation. The same agentic system serves both the seller on the front line and the leader reviewing performance at scale. The agentic system orchestrates a growing portfolio of specialized sub-agents, each owning a distinct capability domain. Among them: the Performance Insights Agent generates natural-language business intelligence narratives from complex sales data, turning raw metrics into actionable seller insights. The Customer Insights Agent assembles a 360-degree view of each customer by synthesizing signals across product usage, support history, contract status, and engagement data, helping sellers understand where a customer is in their journey and what they need next. The Data Insights Agent is a text-to-SQL agent that account teams use to query structured analytics data in plain English without writing a single line of SQL. These three agents are the ones referenced throughout the rest of this post. Coordinating these agents reliably at scale made one thing clear: agentic quality wasn’t an operational concern to manage later. It was the prerequisite for operating. A single degraded sub-agent can silently corrupt every response downstream, and traditional monitoring won’t catch it. That reality made a full lifecycle evaluation framework not optional but necessary. AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the connective tissue powering it, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (safety), Amazon CloudWatch (metrics, alarms, tracing), Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon Redshift (evaluation persistence), Amazon Quick (dashboards), and AWS Lambda (custom evaluators). In this post, we share how we tackled the hardest operational challenges in running AI agents at enterprise scale, and how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations became the backbone of agent quality. Specifically, we cover: Traditional software is deterministic: the same input produces the same output. Machine learning (ML) models introduced probabilistic outputs, and MLOps emerged to manage their training, versioning, monitoring, and re-training. AI agents add a third layer of operational complexity: autonomous, multi-step reasoning, where the question shifts from “did something break?” to “is the agent making sound decisions across its entire reasoning chain?” Agents inherit the hard problems of both predecessors, and introduce some new ones. They’re non-determi
